acceptedWorkstreams.title: Map the cohort software landscape and the searches that actually reach buyers
acceptedWorkstreams.description:
Two questions, answered with evidence rather than with a summary of what everyone already knows.

The first is what the market looks like: which platforms bootcamp operators, training teams and university course leads actually run cohorts on, what each type of platform is structurally good at, where the gaps are, and what a buyer is therefore choosing between. The second is what the searches look like: the intent split behind the head terms, which pages rank for them now, where the real content gaps are, and which long-tail terms are worth building against.

The deliverables are a structured market map organised by platform type with the honest trade-offs of each, a search-intent table with the live evidence, and a prioritised list of terms with the reasoning attached to each one. The output is a positioning brief the marketing work can be built on, not a list of competitor names.

Two rules keep it defensible. Every claim about another product is limited to what that product publicly states about itself, and every search observation is taken from the live results with the source recorded, not from a keyword tool estimate. Where a number cannot be sourced it is left out rather than estimated, because an unsourced number in a competitive brief is worse than no number. The searches also get separated by intent, because 'best platform for online bootcamps' currently returns courses to enrol in and an entirely unrelated piece of software, and treating that as one search is how briefs end up aimed at the wrong reader.

pendingIdeas.title: Measure what AI assistants answer and cite for cohort-platform questions, with dated prompts
pendingIdeas.description: Buyers increasingly ask an assistant instead of scrolling a results page, and nothing in this goal measures that channel. Method: fix ten buyer questions in advance (for example 'best platform to run a bootcamp cohort in Nigeria', 'Slack alternative for a school with 300 students', 'tool for live classes plus file sharing with one cohort'), run the same ten on the same day each month in three assistants, and record the date, every brand named, every URL cited and whether zedu.chat appears at all. Deliver: a dated results table, a share-of-voice count (brand to number of prompts where it is named), the list of cited domains we are absent from, and a month-on-month change log. Already checked on 22 Oct 2026, so the first run has a real baseline: circle.so/llms.txt returns 3.6 KB of text and teachfloor.com/llms.txt returns 14.5 KB, while zedu.chat/llms.txt returns the HTML app shell like every unknown path, so Zedu has no machine-readable summary at all. I am not claiming those files decide AI answers; the audit measures answers, and the files are context only. Done when a reviewer can re-run the ten prompts from the sheet and get a comparable table. Measured by prompts where Zedu is named, and by the cited domains we are missing from.

upvotes.reason: "Measure what AI assistants answer and cite for cohort-platform questions, with dated prompts" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it produces something checkable rather than an opinion, so the goal either moved or it did not.

Re-checked today: circle.so/llms.txt is 3,657 bytes of text/plain, teachfloor.com/llms.txt is 14,484 bytes, and zedu.chat/llms.txt returns the 22 KB text/html app shell with a 200. So the baseline is real and reproducible. None of the goal's nine accepted approaches measures what AI assistants say or cite, so this fills a real gap, and fixed, dated prompts make the result comparable month to month.
